situation:
You are the operations manager at CEDARBROOK CLEAN, a maker of plant-based cleaning concentrates that has run out of the same small plant for three generations. Twenty-eight employees mix, fill and ship every order, and each of them watches a cost line the family put in their hands years ago. The owner (judge), the founder's granddaughter, has asked you to recommend how the company should answer an offer that arrived last week.

Cedarbrook sells to about sixty independent grocers and directly to households through a refill program its customers reorder every few months. The refill program carries the company's name, its own label, and the radio and social advertising the owner (judge) buys each spring. Margins are thin, and half the plant's overhead sits in a second filling line that runs only two days a week.

A regional grocery chain now wants a wholesale account on different terms. It would take the concentrates under its own private label, set the shelf price itself, require exclusive rights to the refill line across the region, and pay ninety days after delivery. The volume would fill the second line five days a week and cover the overhead standing behind it.

Under those terms the Cedarbrook name leaves the shelf, the spring advertising has nothing left to promote, and the chain's auditors would need standing access to a plant floor the company has always kept locked to visitors. Turning the offer down keeps the name, the advertising and the sixty independent grocers, but leaves the second filling line running only two days a week with its overhead unrecovered.

The owner (judge) wants you to analyze what the wholesale account would cost the company beyond price, weigh the revenue it brings against the control it surrenders, and recommend whether Cedarbrook should accept the terms. The owner (judge) will greet you, hear your ideas, ask two questions, and thank you when the presentation and questions are over.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the owner of CEDARBROOK CLEAN and the third generation of the family to run it. Business background is the same as the situation above. You buy the spring advertising yourself, you know every one of the sixty independent grocers by their store, and you also know that a second filling line running two days a week is overhead the company has carried for too long. The regional grocery chain's terms are the largest offer the plant has ever had.

You have asked the operations manager (participant) to analyze what the wholesale account would cost beyond price, weigh the revenue against the control it surrenders, and recommend whether to accept the chain's terms. You want to hear what the ninety day payment terms and the auditors' access to the plant floor would mean for how the plant actually runs.

After the participant has presented, you will ask these two questions:
judgeQuestions: Suppose we turn this down. What are we giving up?
Would we be able to go back to the chain later if we needed to?
